stories.text: Henry Ireton, eldest son of German Ireton of Attenborough, was baptised in St Mary's Church here on 3 November 1611. He fought for Parliament at Edgehill in October 1642. On the night before Naseby, in June 1645, he surprised the Royalist army; the next day he was wounded and captured, and Cromwell later freed him. He married Bridget, Cromwell's eldest daughter, was one of the commissioners who signed the death warrant of Charles I, and died of disease outside Limerick on 26 November 1651.

In St Mary's churchyard a memorial remembers the 134 people killed on 1 July 1918 (137 by another count)[^count] in the explosion at the shell factory in Chilwell, still the largest number of deaths caused by a single explosion in mainland Britain.

37125.sum: St. Mary's Church, Attenborough is a parish church in the Church of England in the village of Attenborough, Nottinghamshire. The church is Grade I listed by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport as a building of outstanding architectural or historic interest.

stories.text: After a riot in Fleet Street, Richard II summoned the mayor, sheriffs and aldermen of London to appear before him and his council at Nottingham Castle on 25 June 1392. The mayor and sheriffs were removed from their offices and imprisoned, and a royal warden was put in charge of the City: London lost its self-government until it had paid the king to win it back.

While Richard I was away, the castle was held by supporters of his brother, Prince John, among them the Sheriff of Nottingham. In March 1194 King Richard came and besieged it, building siege machines like those he had used on crusade.

King John took hostages in numbers no king had before. In 1212, when the Welsh rose against him, he came to Nottingham with his army and, the chronicler Roger of Wendover says, before he either ate or drank had twenty-eight youths hanged, whom he had received from the Welsh as hostages the year before.[^wendover] The Magna Carta Project puts them at some thirty, and calls it notorious.[^mcp]

stories.text: When the House of Lords threw out the Second Reform Bill on 8 October 1831, rioting broke out in Nottingham and a crowd burned the castle, which belonged to the Duke of Newcastle, an opponent of reform. Three men were hanged; the Duke refused to restore the castle, and its burnt shell stood on the rock for years.

After Henry IV's queen, Joan of Navarre, lived here until 1437, the castle was little kept up, until the Wars of the Roses made it a stronghold again.[^s1] Edward IV proclaimed himself king in Nottingham, and in 1476 ordered a new tower and royal apartments, which John Leland, writing in 1540, thought the finest part of the castle.[^s1] On 20 August 1485 Richard III rode from Nottingham to Leicester, two days before he was killed at Bosworth.[^s2]

In 1643 Colonel John Hutchinson took command of Nottingham Castle, and Parliament later made him governor of both town and castle. It was a hard post: the town had no walls, the garrison was small and short of supplies, and the committee that ran the town quarrelled. Hutchinson held on all the same, and protected the radical separatists among his soldiers as far as he could.

The burnt mansion stood a ruin until Thomas Chambers Hine restored it in 1875. The Prince of Wales opened it in 1878 as Nottingham Castle Museum, the first municipal art gallery in the United Kingdom outside London. The castle closed in 2018 for a redevelopment that cost £30 million, and reopened on 21 June 2021 under the charity Nottingham Castle Trust. In November 2022 the trust said it was appointing liquidators, and the site went back to the council.

The first castle on the rock was a wooden motte-and-bailey, begun in 1068 on William the Conqueror's orders, and rebuilt in stone under Henry II. For centuries it was a royal fortress and an occasional royal residence. After the Civil War it was razed in 1651, and in the 1670s the 1st Duke of Newcastle began a mansion on the rock. Rioters burnt the mansion in 1831; it reopened as a museum in 1878.

The Royalists of Newark raided again and again. Sir Charles Lucas broke into the town in January 1644 and tried to set it on fire, and in April 1645 a party from Newark took the fort at Trent Bridge. Each time Hutchinson won back what was lost, and each demand that he surrender the castle he answered with fresh defiance.

A regiment raised in 1741 became, at the request of the people of Nottinghamshire, the 45th (1st Nottinghamshire) Regiment of Foot in 1779.[^s1] Against Napoleon it fought through the Peninsular War from 1808 to 1814, and at Talavera in 1809 won the nickname "Old Stubborns".[^s1] Renamed the Sherwood Foresters in 1866, it was joined with the Derbyshire regiment on 1 July 1881 as the Sherwood Foresters (Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire Regiment), whose museum is in the castle.[^s1]

Henry VIII sent new tapestries ahead of his visit in August 1511, but a survey of 1525 found the castle in "dekay and ruyne", part of the Great Hall's roof fallen in. It was garrisoned again in 1536, against the Pilgrimage of Grace, and in 1562 it was to host a meeting of Elizabeth I and Mary, Queen of Scots, which never took place. By 1600 it was no longer a royal home.

In 1995 the Design Museum in London put on True Brit, a show marking 25 years of the fashion business of Paul Smith, who was born in Beeston. It went on to Glasgow and then to his home city, where it was shown in Nottingham Castle.
Kate Watson Wallis (1852–1918), a suffragist, lived in the Residence at the Castle with her husband, the Castle Art Gallery's first curator.

74050.sum: Nottingham Castle is a Stuart Restoration-era ducal mansion in Nottingham, England, built on the site of a Norman castle built starting in 1068, and added to extensively through the medieval period, when it was an important royal fortress and occasional royal residence. In decline by the 16th century, the original castle, except for its walls and gates, was demolished after the English Civil War in 1651.

stories.text: A church of St Nicholas stood here from the 11th or 12th century. In the Civil War, Royalists took its tower and fired on the castle's garrison, so in 1643 the castle's governor, Colonel John Hutchinson, had it destroyed. For 28 years there was no church here; the brick church standing today was begun in 1671 and finished in 1678.

74093.sum: St Nicholas Church, known locally as St Nic's, is a parish church in Nottingham city centre under the Anglican diocese of Southwell. The church, since 1953, is Grade II* listed by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport as it is a particularly significant building of more than local interest.

stories.text: The first written record of a royal hunting lodge at Bestwood is from 1286, in the reign of Edward I. Charles II and Nell Gwyn visited it, and in 1682 he leased the lodge to her. Their son, Charles Beauclerk, Earl of Burford, was made Duke of St Albans in 1684, and Bestwood passed down through his descendants.

The present lodge was built in 1862–65 for the 10th Duke of St Albans by Samuel Sanders Teulon, in the Gothic Revival style. The army took it over in the Second World War, and in the mid-1970s it became a hotel. It is listed Grade II*.

179201.sum: Bestwood Lodge is a Grade II* listed 19th-century country house in the civil parish of Deer Park, Nottinghamshire, England. It was built in the Gothic Revival style in 1862–65 for the 10th Duke of St Albans by architect Samuel Sanders Teulon. It has been operated as the Bestwood Lodge Hotel since the 1970s.

In 1947 the Trent flooded 3,000 properties, 86 factories and 28 miles of road in Nottingham, and the city's first flood defence was built that year. Photographs of West Bridgford under water are in Inspire Picture Archive. A new defence along 27 km of the river, from Sawley to Colwick, was finished in 2012.

stories.text: The medieval bridge had a chapel of St James at one end and was kept by a religious house, until on 21 February 1551 a royal charter passed its repair to the Corporation, with lands to pay for it, the Bridge Estate. Floods damaged it again and again, and in 1683 they swept away its northern half. Rebuilt with fifteen arches, 538 ft long in all, it stood until its foundations grew unsafe, and in the 1860s a new bridge was begun.

In 1156 a stone bridge of more than 20 arches was begun here. It was known as the Hethbeth bridge, and two of its arches survive on the south bank. The present iron bridge nearby was designed by Marriott Ogle Tarbotton, built between 1868 and 1871, and widened to 80 feet in 1924–26.

Marriott Ogle Tarbotton was Nottingham's Borough Engineer from 1859. He designed Trent Bridge, planned the town's underground sewers, culverted the River Leen and built the viaduct over the railway on Carrington Street in 1866.

303808.sum: Trent Bridge is an iron and stone road bridge across the River Trent in Nottingham, England. It is the principal river crossing for entrance to the city from the south, although the upstream Clifton Bridge is both larger and busier.

stories.text: John Hutchinson, born at Owthorpe in 1615, held Nottingham Castle for Parliament from 1643 and signed Charles I's death warrant.[^s1] He died a prisoner in 1664 and is buried at Owthorpe; his wife Lucy's Memoirs of his life made him famous.[^s1]

320958.sum: St Margaret's Church, Owthorpe is a Grade II* listed parish church in the Church of England in Owthorpe, Nottinghamshire, England. Owthorpe has an unusual Grade II* listed Anglican church, dedicated to St Margaret of Antioch, once considered a patron saint of pregnancy. It stands away from the village in farmland, surrounded by a low wall, next to the site where the manor stood.
